**National goal:** The Strategy aims to prevent food loss and waste, increase recycling of food and other organic materials to support a more circular economy, reduce GHG emissions, save households and businesses money, and build cleaner, healthier communities [6]. Its actions are meant to help the U.S. meet its National Food Loss and Waste Reduction Goal — to halve food loss and waste by 2030 — and contribute to the National Recycling Goal of a 50% recycling rate by 2030, as well as UN SDG Target 12.3 [6]. The 50%-by-2030 goal was jointly announced by EPA and USDA in 2015, and in 2021 EPA aligned the food waste portion with SDG Target 12.3 [8].

**Food's share of landfilled MSW and landfill methane:**
- Food is the single most common material in landfills, making up **24% of municipal solid waste in landfills** [9].
- Food waste is responsible for **58% of landfill methane emissions** released to the atmosphere [8]. Separately, the Strategy states that **61% of methane generated by landfilled food waste is not captured** by landfill gas collection systems and is released to the atmosphere [9].

Note that the 58% figure refers to food waste's share of landfill methane emissions, while the 61% figure refers to the uncaptured portion of methane generated by landfilled food waste — these are distinct measures [8][9].

meet its National Food Loss and Waste Reduction Goal — to halve food loss and waste by 2030 — and contribute to the National Recycling Goal of a 50% recycling rate by 2030, as well as UN SDG Target 12.3.

Food is the single most common material in landfills, making up **24% of municipal solid waste in landfills**.
Food waste is responsible for **58% of landfill methane emissions** released to the atmosphere.
Separately, the Strategy states that **61% of methane generated by landfilled food waste is not captured** by landfill gas collection systems and is released to the atmosphere.

## LTC reasons for pre-made products [1]

| Reason | % |
|---|---|

| Less culinary skill required of staff | 46% |
| Able to serve items difficult to make | 39% |
| Staff has more time for other tasks | 30% |

Note the tension: **cost** is the leading scratch driver (59%) but a weak pre-made driver (16%); **consistency** and **skill avoidance** dominate the pre-made case (51%, 46%) [1].

## How this relates to the Segment Guide

- Prep in healthcare "tends to be more focused on scratch," because kitchens manage multiple specific diets and are less able to rely on prepared or semi-prepared items that may not meet nutritional or ingredient guidelines [2].
- Culinary skill is described as **moderate**; hospital and LTC menus are generally simple and limited, so most hospital and LTC kitchens "don't need high levels of culinary skill" [2]. Limited culinary skill also appears as an operator pain point [3].
- For hospitals and LTC the priority is serving relatively healthful food to many patients/residents in a short window; **ease of prep** matters, as do dishes that hold well over long journeys from kitchen to room [2].
- Consumer expectations lean toward fresh/made-to-order (LTC 69%) and catering to specific diets (LTC 69%), with variety at 71% [5].

The two sources are consistent rather than contradictory: scratch is the default posture, driven by diet specificity and cost, while pre-made is valued for consistency and for compensating for moderate skill and time pressure [1][2].

## Implication for a supplier of sauces, bases and soups

- **Position as scratch-enabling, not scratch-replacing.** The scratch case rests on cost, quality and cross-application use [1], and the segment's stated reason for scratch is diet compliance [2]. A base or soup that lets a moderate-skill kitchen finish a dish itself speaks to both.
- **Lead with consistency and labour savings.** These are the two strongest pre-made drivers (51% and 46%) [1] and map directly onto the documented moderate culinary skill and ease-of-prep priority [2][3].
- **Address diet specificity head-on.** Because operators avoid prepared items that may not meet nutritional or ingredient guidelines [2], formulations and documentation around low-sodium, diabetic-friendly and similar diets are the key barrier to overcome.
- **Sell hold time and speed of service.** Dishes must hold well over the journey from kitchen to patient room and be served to many people in a short window [2].
- **Sauces, gravies and soups are named menu parts in the PULSE scratch-usage breakdown** [1], so they sit precisely where the scratch/pre-made decision is being made.
- **Expect price sensitivity.** Cost is the top scratch benefit [1] and affordability is a top consumer want across facility types (LTC 70%) [5], so value framing matters.

**Caveat:** the context gives no hospital-specific scratch/pre-made reason data, no purchase-volume data for sauces/bases/soups, and no operator willingness-to-pay figures, so the commercial sizing of this opportunity cannot be assessed from these passages.
